prohibited_recommendations: Do not delay treatment based on sensory predominance — sensory-variant GBS is well-described.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
required_recommendations: Initiate IVIG / plasma exchange even with sensory-predominant presentation if areflexia and CSF dissociation present.
Repeat EMG / NCS at 7–14 days if initial study is borderline.
Broader panels (paraneoplastic, Sjögren) if pattern remains atypical.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, early AIDP with sensory-predominant presentation

differential.key_features: Subacute sensory predominance; paraneoplastic and Sjögren panels distinguish; EMG distinguishes ganglionopathy from radiculoneuropathy.
Levels, MMA / homocysteine, posterior column predominance.
Chronic length-dependent; would not explain acute progression and areflexia with CSF dissociation.

key_clinical_evidence: Sensory-variant GBS has acute progression, areflexia, and elevated CSF protein but may lack overt weakness — diagnosis rests on these supportive features.
Distinction from paraneoplastic sensory ganglionopathy is by EMG pattern (radicular versus ganglionopathic SNAP loss) and serology.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

past_medical_history: Resected colon adenocarcinoma (2015, no active disease)

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. E. is a 75-year-old woman with a history of remote colon cancer resection, cervical canal stenosis, longstanding right foot drop, and recent atrial fibrillation who was brought to the emergency department after waking from sleep with left hand numbness and bilateral foot paresthesias. She was immediately triaged as a stroke thrombolysis candidate given the abrupt onset. However, she was ineligible for IV tPA because the exact time of symptom onset was unknown (wake-up stroke criteria not met). CT brain and CT angiography showed no hemorrhage and no proximal vascular occlusion. Initial examination showed decreased sensation in her left hand and bilateral forefeet in a non-dermatomal distribution. Reflexes were normal on initial assessment. She was admitted for MRI brain to complete the stroke workup. Critically, she was unable to mobilize independently despite having relatively preserved motor strength in most muscle groups — this mismatch raised concern. Two weeks prior to presentation, she had experienced 2-3 days of cough, fever, and myalgias that resolved spontaneously. She has multiple background diagnoses (cervical stenosis, chronic right foot drop, prior cancer) that could individually explain isolated findings. The symptoms were in a non-dermatomal sensory pattern, progressive over hours, and followed a prior viral illness; the presentation lacked the classic ascending paralysis pattern. Reflexes were normal on the first examination, and areflexia developed only on subsequent day 2 assessment.
